source.title: There Is More to Refusal in Large Language Models than a Single Direction
source.authors: Faaiz Joad; Majd Hawasly; Sabri Boughorbel; Nadir Durrani; H. Sencar

record.tranche_reason: The study measures difference-of-means refusal directions, intervenes by steering and ablation, and reports that directions can be geometrically distinct while their behavioral effects share a control pattern. Its results refine and qualify the single-direction account.
record.gate_note: Reports intervention outcomes and geometry relevant to V1 and V4. Values used only to select layers, positions, steering strengths, and SAE latent counts are not recorded as results. Cited findings from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: Builds difference-in-means refusal directions from 11 refusal splits in three 7–9B instruct models. It measures refusal and over-refusal under steering and ablation, and reports geometry and cross-direction ablation. It argues explicitly that the single-direction account is incomplete. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors also conclude that safety-direction ablation removes safety refusals but leaves CoCoNot non-safety refusals at about 0.3–0.5, and that individual split directions transfer poorly under ablation while diverse-source directions ablate broadly (a shared refusal core). They limit the claims to 7–9B instruct decoder models.
record.recipe_differences: Uses harmful-refused versus benign-complied activation differences and residual-stream steering/ablation, but learns directions across broader refusal categories and uses selected hook positions. Ablation is applied across residual-stream layers at the chosen token position, not every position.
record.method_sensitivity: Direction category affects geometry and refusal style; safety/content-policy directions reach saturation at lower steering strengths than capability and underspecification directions. Model and split also affect ablation outcomes. Tested steering strengths and hook choices were selected using validation or sweeps.

fits_no_version.finding: Steering along different split directions yields different dominant refusal rationales (capability, underspecification, safety) at similar refusal rates (Tables 4, 5, 29). SAE analysis finds a shared core of about 5% of latents plus split-specific latents.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Distinct refusal directions control the style or rationale of refusal rather than its rate, built on a shared core of refusal features.

record.problems: Three instruction-tuned models, roughly 7B–9B; no base models or larger models. The main activation-space behavioral outcomes are judged by WildGuard, with manual validation and a separate reported human comparison. Some cross-model ablation comparisons use a prompt pool selected using Gemma's baseline behavior. Controlled accuracy is not a broad general-capability evaluation. The authors state that interventions are not intended to establish causal mediation.
record.rows_left_out: The paper also reports activation-steering outcomes for Qwen in Table 1, detailed steering-strength sweeps (including Tables 10–13 and Figure 11), SAE steering and SAE ablation analyses (including Tables 3, 12, and 13), and extensive per-direction unified-pool ablation results (Tables 22–25). These were not included because the retained rows prioritize the main activation-space steering and safety-direction ablation results plus the cross-split geometry and mixed-source ablation result.

untested.parts: Preservation of general capabilities: Acc on the balanced controlled set is not a capability benchmark. Geometry is reported for Gemma only.
No weight-edit or abliteration of released models.
No jailbreak analysis or adversarial training.
Harmfulness versus refusal encoding is not tested; it is only cited.
No cross-language, cross-variant or base-to-instruct transfer.

record.verdict_notes: Table 2's last row is labelled a round-robin direction, but its values match Curated-32 (Qwen) and Crisp best-seed (Gemma, Llama) in Tables 23–25; the RR-33 means are much lower. Table 2's Llama XSTest value (32.9) differs from Table 25 (39.8). Results declared in rows_left_out bear on V1/V4 and should be added as rows: Qwen Incomplete-CCN steering shows no induction (RR 0.50, ORR 0.47; Table 1). Per-split unified-pool ablation is near zero for all 11 Gemma directions (<15%; Table 24). Table 22 also covers a fourth model, Qwen-1.8B. The authors state that the interventions are not meant to establish causal mediation. The ablation conclusion for Llama and Qwen rests on a Gemma-filtered pool.

versions.untested_parts: Tests split-specific harmful/refusal-versus-benign/compliance directions, steering, and ablation. It does not test ablation at every position; ablation is applied at selected token positions, although across residual-stream layers. It does not establish causal mediation (the authors explicitly say the interventions are not intended to establish it), or assess broad general capabilities beyond the controlled evaluation metrics.
No released-model weight-edit or abliteration procedure is evaluated.
Does not test whether jailbreaks suppress the direction or whether training against ablation improves robustness.
Tests distinct difference-of-means directions, intervention effects, and shared versus category-specific refusal components. It does not establish a complete affine or cone account.
Does not directly test whether harmfulness judgment is represented separately from the refusal decision.
Uses three instruction-tuned models, but does not transfer a direction across languages, model variants, or from base to instruct models.
Does not vary how or when refusal training is conducted.

source_check.notes: The call line's capability=y is wrong: the study has no capability measure, and Acc is refusal accuracy. Table 2's 'RR' row matches Curated-32 (Qwen 87.1) and Crisp best seed (Gemma 81.1, Llama 69.5) in Tables 23-25, not RR-33 (means 35.0/45.8/37.9). Table 1 disagrees with Table 11 (α=100) on some Gemma splits, and Table 2's XSTest cells disagree with Tables 23-25.

statements.correction: Gemma (baseline RR 1.00 by construction): non-safety CCN RR 0.34-0.45 after ablation. Llama 0.11-0.49 and Qwen 0.15-0.47 on Gemma-refused prompts, no own baseline. Llama Safety-CCN 0.43 and OverRefusal-XST 0.30 show incomplete removal within safety-type refusal, with the same caveat.
statements.problem: Numbers right, but Llama/Qwen values are post-ablation on a Gemma-filtered pool with no within-model baseline, so 'keeps'/'persist' is unmeasured for them. Safety-CCN and XSTest are safety-type splits, not other refusal types.

statements.correction: 2602.02132: preprint; gemma-2-9b-it, Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen-7B-Chat. Controls are random-latent and random-vector (SAE steering). Std over prompts and seeds. WildGuard judge, kappa 0.93 vs humans. No capability benchmark. Ablation at all layers; steering at one layer.
statements.problem: This study has no capability check: Acc is refusal accuracy on the balanced set. Its ablation runs at every layer, not a single layer. The 2602.02132 part of 'what' is cut off in the pack.

statements.correction: At selected alpha (Gemma 100, Llama 2.5), RR/ORR are near-identical (Table 1), except Llama Incomplete-CCN RR 0.65, ORR 0.70. At Gemma alpha=30, ORR is 0.38 for Humanizing-CCN vs 0.82 for Advice-SB (Table 11): safety-cluster directions saturate sooner.
statements.problem: Near-identical RR/ORR holds only at the selected near-saturating alpha. Appendix L says the curves remain distinguishable at moderate strength. Llama Incomplete-CCN is an exception.

statements.correction: Under ablation, distinct per-split directions differ widely: Table 2 de-refusal is Gemma 0.0-14.1%, Qwen 0.9-73.5%, Llama 14.1-39.1%. Under steering at the selected alpha, they give near-identical RR/ORR (Table 1).
statements.problem: Steering similarity holds at saturating alpha only (Appendix L). The ablation side uses one safety direction, not the distinct directions; the per-split ablation contrast is the stronger evidence.
